The time-of-day clock does not count the processor clock. The data sheet says it "requires an external 60 Hz or 50 Hz (programmable) TTL level input on the TOD pin", and control register A's bit 7 chooses which. On the C64 that signal comes from the mains. *The Transactor*'s 1985 tour of the C64's circuit board traced it: the 9 volt AC supply from the power pack is "the source of the 60 Hz signal used by the time-of-day (TOD) clock", squared up by a logic gate and fed to both CIAs. The SX-64 portable has a switching power supply and no AC line, so, the magazine noted, it carries "an additional oscillator circuit, including another crystal" just to supply the TOD signal.

context: Texas Instruments used the word in the data manual for its TMS9918 video chip, which went into the TI-99/4A, the [ColecoVision](/vault/systems/colecovision) and [MSX](/vault/systems/msx) computers. Its glossary defines a sprite as "an object whose pattern is relative to a specified X, Y coordinate and whose position can therefore be controlled by that coordinate with a positional resolution of one pixel". Karl Guttag, who designed the chip's sprite logic, has written that "the 9918 coined the word 'Sprites'", and credits the name to his colleague Dave Ackley.

Texas Instruments' TMS9918 family, the video chips of the TI-99/4A, the ColecoVision (which used the TMS9928) and MSX computers, set the pattern. "Only four sprites can be active on any horizontal line," says the 1982 data manual; the four highest-priority sprites are drawn, and "the fifth and subsequent sprites are not displayed on that line." The chip also sets a flag in its status register and stores the number of the fifth sprite, so a program can find out which sprite broke the rule.

context: "You can tell a Llamasoft game by just one glance at the screen," Jeff Minter wrote in the first issue of *Zzap!64*, in May 1985. He was 23, had been selling games under the Llamasoft name for three years, and was explaining why. "When I write a game, I'm writing for those people who like my game style." That style (fast shooting, pulsing colour, llamas, camels and sheep, and a running commentary from the author) stayed recognisable across the VIC-20, the Commodore 64, the Atari ST, the Atari Jaguar and the consoles that followed.

"I'd never done any 3D at that point and never so much as touched a polygon," [Jeff Minter](/vault/people/jeff-minter) told *Edge*, looking back on the day he volunteered to remake *[Tempest](/vault/games/tempest)*. Atari had gathered developers at a hotel near Heathrow to show off its new Jaguar console and read out a list of old games it owned and wanted converting. When *Tempest* came up, Minter put his hand up. The result was a game in which Dave Theurer's glowing wireframe tube became a shaded web that swung about the screen, enemies shattered into clouds of particles, and a booming voice announced "Excellent!" over pounding techno. *Edge* called it "one of the best all-out blasters ever created". For many owners of Atari's struggling console, it was the reason they had bought one.

"As aficionados of the game will confirm, the best way to play Doom is with a mouse and keyboard. Over the next seven years console developers stopped apologising for the joypad and built games around it, with auto-aim, an analogue stick for each hand and split-screen matches for four players on one television.

Atari's guide described the way round it in 1979. A game that moved its objects with fractional speeds held in tables, "2 byte fractional addition techniques (or anything not based on frames per second)", could be converted by "changing the fraction tables, avoiding major surgery on the program". A converted game moves its objects a little further each frame to cover the same distance per second. That took time, and the extra lines of a PAL frame could cost more. *Edge* explained in 1994 that "programmers can often turn up the game speed in their code", but that the taller PAL picture meant "a greater drain on the processor, making a full speed conversion hard to achieve". Its example was the Jaguar's *Cybermorph*, which ran "about 3-4% slower on a PAL Jaguar than on an NTSC model", not 17 per cent, because its updates were not tied to the frame.

context: A digital joystick is four switches. Push it and the program learns which way, and nothing else.
